snippet.description:
This documentary unveils the monumental engineering and scandalous history behind the Château de Chambord, a structure so ambitious it was once deemed impossible. Commissioned by the young, visionary King Francis I and designed in collaboration with the legendary Leonardo da Vinci, this "stone giant" was built on a treacherous swamp using revolutionary 3D-like geometry, including its famous double-helix staircase. From hiding the Mona Lisa during WWII to bankrupting the French treasury, the video explores the construction secrets, the "coded messages" in its architecture, and the 500-year-old mystery of its missing floor plans.

snippet.title: 1618-1648: The Bloody History of the 30 Years War
snippet.description:
In 1618, a brilliant comet tore across the European sky - an omen so bright it was visible during the day. Men saw it as a whip wielded by God to punish humanity. What followed was the Thirty Years' War: the bloodiest conflict the world had ever seen up to that point, and the first "modern" war in human history. Through the rare, surviving diaries of ordinary soldiers, orphaned noblewomen, and the shadowy machinations of master politicians like Cardinal Richelieu and Father Joseph, this documentary uncovers the sheer brutality of a war that claimed millions of lives.

snippet.title: The Untold Stories of the KGB
snippet.description:
For over a century, Russian history has been shaped by the shadow of its secret police. From Lenin’s Cheka and Stalin’s brutal purges to the Cold War spy games of the KGB and the modern-day FSB, Russia’s security network has outlived communism itself. This feature-length documentary uncovers the dark history of the world's most powerful secret service, told through the firsthand accounts of both the veterans who served it and the victims who survived it. Explore how a lowly lieutenant colonel rose to the Kremlin, how radioactive poison and cyber warfare became modern tools of statecraft, and why in today's Russia, it is no longer a state with a security service—but a security service with a state.

snippet.title: The Strange Algorithm People Used To Run Their Lives
snippet.description:
The  1970s were a decade packed with real scientific breakthroughs; NASA launched Voyager 1, Intel revolutionized computing with the first microprocessor, and JVC introduced the VHS. At the same time, some more -- shall we say -- outside-the-box ideas also started quietly gaining traction, ideas like biorhythms. Promoted as a scientific way to predict your physical, emotional, and intellectual highs and lows, biorhythms captured the public's imagination... but were they really all that?

On this episode of Weird History, we dive into one of the strangest fads of the seventies' new age movement and try to determine whether it was legit science or just pseudoscience dressed up in math. 

And have you ever had a biorhythm reading? Let us know in the comments!

snippet.title: Why America celebrates the ‘WRONG’ Independence Day
snippet.description:
Every year, Americans mark the Fourth of July with fireworks, parades and celebrations. Subscribe here: https://bit.ly/subhistoryextrayoutube

But the vote to break away from Britain actually took place two days earlier, on 2 July 1776.

So why did one date become America's national holiday while the other faded into the background? In this episode, HistoryExtra’s Elinor Evans explores the dramatic story behind the United States Declaration of Independence, and asks why this document became far more important than the vote itself.

Featuring insights from historian and broadcaster Professor Adam IP Smith and historian George Goodwin, this episode examines how independence emerged from years of growing tensions between Britain and its American colonies, and why the Declaration continues to resonate nearly 250 years later.

snippet.title: What Daily Life Was REALLY Like for Ordinary Americans in 1940 | Boring History For Sleep
snippet.description:
Tonight, we step quietly into America in 1940 — a year balanced between recovery and uncertainty.

This video explores what daily life was really like for ordinary Americans during the last peaceful months before the United States entered World War II. The Great Depression was beginning to loosen its grip. Radios filled homes with comedy and music. New appliances slowly appeared in shops and advertisements. Yet beyond daily routines, war in Europe cast a distant shadow, bringing quiet debate, anxious headlines, and a vague sense that the world was changing.

This is not a history lesson of speeches and battles. It is a calm, immersive journey through a single ordinary day — experienced through routine, work, home life, and the slow rhythm of a society standing at the edge of a new era.


Designed for relaxation, background listening, and sleep, this video moves slowly and without urgency. There are no sudden sounds, no dramatic turns — only calm storytelling and the quiet details of everyday life in 1940.

If you enjoy boring history for sleep, immersive everyday life history, and long-form calm storytelling, this episode is meant to be listened to gently.

snippet.title: Vincenzo Peruggia: The Man Who Stole The Mona Lisa
snippet.description:
In 1911, the world was rocked by the "unimaginable" news: the Mona Lisa had been stolen from the Louvre. For over two years, the masterpiece was truly gone, leaving the "greatest detectives in the world" clueless and leading to the interrogation of famous figures like Pablo Picasso. In this documentary, we retrace the footsteps of Vincenzo Peruggia, the house painter who walked out of the museum with Da Vinci’s treasure wrapped in his smock. Through exclusive interviews with Peruggia’s 84-year-old daughter, Celestina, and access to long-lost psychiatric reports and personal letters, we strip away the myths.

snippet.title: What Daily Life Was REALLY Like Before Electricity in 1700s America | Boring History For Sleep
snippet.description:
Tonight, we step quietly into 1700s America — a time before electricity, modern conveniences, or the noise of machines.

This video explores how people really lived in colonial America, focusing on daily life before the advent of electrical power. From the moment the sun rose to the time the hearth fire was dimmed, life was shaped by manual labor, daylight, and fire. Homes were lit by candles and hearths, food was preserved only through laborious methods, and tasks like cooking and cleaning were long, physical endeavors.

In this immersive, calm journey, you’ll explore:
– Early morning routines without modern lighting or appliances  
– Heating the home with firewood, and cooking over an open flame  
– The slow rhythms of daily chores: washing, mending, and tending to the farm  
– The quiet of the night when artificial light was a luxury  
– The profound reliance on daylight and the natural world for survival  

This video is designed for relaxation, background listening, and sleep. The pace is slow, with no sudden noises or dramatic shifts, only steady narration and sensory details that gently guide you into a restful state.

snippet.title: How Did Frozen Water Become the World's Most Unlikely Luxury?
snippet.description:
In 1833, a ship arrived in Calcutta carrying something no one in India had ever seen. Massive blocks of ice, clear as crystal, still frozen after a voyage of 16,000 miles across the equator. The crowd on the dock wept to touch it. They called it a miracle.

But the man who sent it, Frederic Tudor, was not a miracle worker. He was a stubborn Boston businessman who had spent 27 years failing. His family called him a fool. The newspapers called his ice scheme "Tudor's Folly." He went bankrupt. He went to debtor's prison. And every time the world told him to quit, he doubled down.

This is the story of how frozen water, something that literally fell from the sky for free every winter in Massachusetts, became a luxury worth more than gold. It is the story of how one man's obsession created the global cold chain, the multi-trillion-dollar infrastructure of refrigerated ships and trucks and warehouses that keeps our food fresh and our medicine viable today. And it is the story of how we forgot the Ice King entirely, even as we use his invention every single day.

From the frozen ponds of New England to the sweltering docks of Calcutta, from debtor's prison to a monopoly on cold itself, this is the untold story of the Victorian ice trade.

Thank you to Halara for sponsoring my video. You can use my code ivy for 20% off all regular priced items or if you’re in the U.S. ivy12 for 12% off all items including things on sale. 

In this video you will explore historical sportswear from around the turn of the century. Starting with a 19th century Victorian tennis outfit, an 1890s cycling outfit with split skirt and authentic sweater reproduced from an original 1890’s design, a whimsical rollerskating outfit and fashionable bathing costume also from the 1890s, and finally a golfing outfit from the early 1900s.  

Seeing how these fashions moved on a real body gives us a unique insight into these garments that can’t be gleaned from simply looking at fashion plates or museum pieces on mannequins. This is especially essential in the case of sportswear, which cannot really be understood when it’s not in motion. 

Be sure to subscribe for part two to see me rollerskating, (mini) golfing, playing tennis and even swimming in my historical clothes.
